<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#Sx1.SS7" title="In Appendix ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">9.7 </span>Distinctions and Advantages of Continual-NExT</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#Sx1.SS8" title="In Appendix ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">9.8 </span>Additional Experiments</span></a></li>
</ol></nav>
</nav>

<div class="ltx_authors">

</span><span id="id4" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_note ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Project Leader</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Dual-to-Dual MLLMs refer to Multimodal Large Language Models, which can enable unified multimodal comprehension and generation through text and image modalities. Although exhibiting strong instantaneous learning and generalization capabilities, Dual-to-Dual MLLMs still remain deficient in lifelong evolution, significantly affecting continual adaptation to dynamic real-world scenarios. One of the challenges is that learning new tasks inevitably destroys the learned knowledge. Beyond traditional catastrophic forgetting, Dual-to-Dual MLLMs face other challenges, including hallucination, instruction unfollowing, and failures in cross-modal knowledge transfer. However, no standardized continual learning framework for Dual-to-Dual MLLMs has been established yet, leaving these challenges unexplored. Thus, in this paper, we establish <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Continual-NExT</span>, a continual learning framework for Dual-to-Dual MLLMs with deliberately-architected evaluation metrics. To improve the continual learning capability of Dual-to-Dual MLLMs, we propose an efficient <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MAGE</span> (<span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">M</span>ixture and <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">A</span>ggregation of <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">G</span>eneral LoRA and <span id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">E</span>xpert LoRA) method to further facilitate knowledge transfer across modalities and mitigate forgetting. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MAGE outperforms other continual learning methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18055v1/Figure1.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/236;" width="429" height="236" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Continual-NExT: A framework for lifelong multimodal learning in Dual-to-Dual MLLMs. The left part shows its multimodal generation capability. The middle part illustrates its development across diverse training stages. The right part presents its supported downstream tasks.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panagopoulou et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> have gradually evolved from visual question answering to multimodal comprehension and generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Dual-to-Dual MLLMs can accept inputs in text/image modality and deliver responses in appropriate text/image feedback <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ge et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>. However, real-world scenarios are characterized by continuously evolving tasks and shifting data distributions. Thus, confronted with these dynamic scenarios, a one-time training paradigm is insufficient. Enhancing the continual learning capability of Dual-to-Dual MLLMs, therefore, becomes increasingly critical <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhai et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luo et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ke et al. (2021)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Traditional continual learning frameworks for MLLMs predominantly concentrate on improving the text generation capabilities of MLLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, with limited exploration of image and text-image hybrid generation. While continual learning has been extensively studied in text-only generation settings, extending it to Dual-to-Dual MLLMs introduces a less explored but fundamental question: <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Do multimodal comprehension and generation inherently conflict under continual learning<span id="S1.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">?</span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To answer the question, in this paper, we propose <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Continual-NExT</span>, the first unified comprehension and generation continual learning framework, as shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Continual-NExT encompasses a variety of multimodal input-output tasks, making it more aligned with real-world scenarios and enabling evaluation of Dual-to-Dual MLLMs’ capability to continually adapt to a wide range of comprehension and generation tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Based on this framework, we investigate catastrophic forgetting and associated challenges <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goodfellow et al., 2013</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">de Masson D’Autume et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. A common intuition is that comprehension and generation represent fundamentally different learning objectives, potentially requiring separate continual learning strategies. However, we discover that the challenge does not stem from the task type itself, but from the asymmetric requirements imposed by input and output modalities. In particular, comprehension tasks primarily rely on stable multimodal representations at the input side, whereas generation tasks demand higher adaptability in modality-specific decoding and reasoning components. In continual learning, these asymmetric requirements lead to distinct forgetting behaviors, even within a single unified model. This observation suggests that the tension between comprehension and generation is not intrinsic, but rather emerges from how model parameters are updated in response to modality-specific inputs and outputs over time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, we propose a novel continual learning method: MAGE (<span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">M</span>ixture and <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">A</span>ggregation of <span id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">G</span>eneral LoRA and <span id="S1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">E</span>xpert LoRA). MAGE efficiently inserts trainable LoRA into the frozen LLM and adopts a well-designed collaborative strategy to merge distinct LoRA experts. Among them, General LoRA is responsible for understanding input modalities, and Expert LoRA handles the reasoning of output modalities. Experimental results demonstrate that MAGE significantly enhances the continual learning capabilities of Dual-to-Dual MLLMs. Our contributions are as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">•We first present a unified comprehension and generation framework (UCL) with well-defined evaluation metrics, serving to evaluate continual learning performance of Dual-to-Dual MLLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">•We introduce an efficient MAGE method that seamlessly integrates General LoRA and Expert LoRA to enhance UCL performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">•Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficiency of MAGE on the Continual-NExT framework that outperforms other state-of-the-art continual learning methods.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dual-to-Dual MLLMs:</span> Conventional MLLMs, such as BLIP-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and Qwen-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, only grasp multimodal comprehension abilities, while lacking multimodal generation abilities. To address this limitation, SEED-X introduces an image discretization tokenizer that encodes visual inputs into discrete tokens with dynamic resolution, facilitating multiscale image understanding and generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ge et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>. NExT-GPT integrates multimodal adapters with various diffusion decoders, allowing it to process inputs and produce outputs across text and image modalities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. AnyGPT employs specialized tokenizers to condense multimodal data, enabling a single autoregressive LLM to handle diverse tasks at the semantic level <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Continual Learning:</span> Traditional continual learning focuses on task-, class-, and domain-incremental learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Van de Ven and Tolias, 2019</a>)</cite>. Recently, continual instruction tuning frameworks have been proposed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and catastrophic forgetting alleviation methods for MLLMs have been explored, including FwT-Prompt employing gradient projection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and CIA implementing dynamic updates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. The above frameworks and methods are exclusively based on Dual-to-Text MLLMs. However, continual learning frameworks and methods specifically designed for Dual-to-Dual MLLMs are still blank.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dual-to-Dual MLLMs Continual Learning</span>: UCL is defined to continually tune Dual-to-Dual MLLMs on new tasks without costly re-training. Compared with traditional continual learning, UCL differs in that it has multimodal inputs and outputs, along with requirements to handle a range of perception and generation tasks. In UCL framework, each incremental task is an independent dataset and focuses on a specific ability. UCL is described as a sequence of tasks <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}_{\text{seq}}=\{t_{1},...,t_{T}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mtext>seq</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}_{\text{seq}}=\{t_{1},...,t_{T}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Each task <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{j}\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{seq}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mtext>seq</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{j}\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{seq}}</annotation></semantics></math> consists of a training set <math id="S2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}^{t_{j}}_{train}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}^{t_{j}}_{train}</annotation></semantics></math> and a test set <math id="S2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}^{t_{j}}_{test}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}^{t_{j}}_{test}</annotation></semantics></math>. The primary goal of UCL is to sequentially learn from <math id="S2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}_{\text{seq}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mtext>seq</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}_{\text{seq}}</annotation></semantics></math> while maintaining the balance between plasticity (adaptation to new tasks) and stability (preservation of prior knowledge).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18055v1/Figure2.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:499/328;" width="499" height="328" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of Continual-NExT, including tasks, task types, sizes, and examples.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Task Settings in Continual-NExT</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Continual-NExT includes six tasks: Visual Question Answering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goyal et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, Image Classification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite>, Image Generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Plummer et al., 2015</a>)</cite>, OCR Token Recognition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mishra et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, Visual Grounding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kazemzadeh et al., 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mao et al., 2016</a>)</cite>, and Image Editing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hui et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Their diversity across modalities and domains ensures a robust evaluation of multimodal comprehension and generation capabilities. We construct the instructions of text generation tasks (<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, VQAv2, Imagenet-1K, OCRVQA, and RefCOCO) by following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Additionally, we adopt the self-made instructions in image generation tasks (<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, Flickr30K and HQEdit). Instructions, data, and statistical details of each task are illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Method ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. The amount of training data in each task is varied, ranging from 10K to 100K, which simulates the randomness of data distribution in the real world. (Detailed information of each task is in Appendix <a href="#Sx1.SS1" title="9.1 Task and Dataset Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Advanced Evaluation Scenarios</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We utilize popular evaluation protocols <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, including Average Accuracy (Avg.Acc), Forgetting, and New Accuracy (New.Acc). For evaluating on text generation tasks, Accuracy is calculated by directly comparing the predictions with labels <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. For evaluating on image generation tasks, Accuracy is calculated by employing the CLIP Score <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hessel et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. We discover that forgetting in UCL is mainly caused by hallucination, instruction unfollowing, and the other errors. Thus, we introduce three diagnostic evaluation metrics to better analyze forgetting behaviors. Specifically, we define the Average Hallucination Rate (Avg.HAL) to depict hallucination-related forgetting, the Average Instruction-Unfollowing Rate (Avg.IUF) to show instruction unfollowing-related forgetting, and the Average Other Error Rate (Avg.OTH) to summarize the other errors-related forgetting (Metrics calculation can be found in Appendix <a href="#Sx1.SS2" title="9.2 Metric Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Discussion<span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">:</span></span> Existing continual learning frameworks for MLLMs mainly rely on engineering-driven unification of data or instruction templates, providing limited insight into the mechanisms of forgetting across heterogeneous tasks. In contrast, Continual-NExT is not merely a collection of multimodal tasks, but a framework designed to expose and evaluate how different input-output modality combinations induce distinct patterns of forgetting and transfer within a unified model.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>MAGE: An Efficient UCL Framework</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Motivation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Existing research shows that the model focuses on different input patterns at each layer, indicating that the model updates its parameters in response to task-specific inputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Voita et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. However, it is unknown <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">whether the model updates its parameters in response to both task-specific inputs and outputs.</span> To answer the question, we fine-tune SEED-X <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ge et al. (2024b)</a></cite> using LoRA and analyze the parameter update patterns across tasks, as shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Motivation ‣ 4 MAGE: An Efficient UCL Framework ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. We select VQAv2 as the first task, followed by five distinct tasks as the second task, including ImageNet, Grounding, OCRVQA (image and text as inputs, text as outputs), Flickr30k (text as inputs, image as outputs), and HQEdit (image and text as inputs, image as outputs). We visualize the absolute discrepancy between the parameters learned from Task 1 and Task 2 and depict heat maps.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18055v1/motivation.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/226;" width="429" height="226" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Parameter update patterns across heterogeneous tasks from global output view (left) to local input view (right). VQAv2-&gt;ImageNet refers to first training on VQAv2 (Task 1) and then training on ImageNet (Task 2). Pixel value represents the absolute discrepancy between the parameters learned from Task 1 and Task 2.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For input-related patterns, we analyze the absolute discrepancy in the shallow (the former 50%) layers according to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alzubaidi et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Tasks using both text and image inputs (<span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, ImageNet, Grounding, OCRVQA) show high discrepancies across most parameters, indicating the need for both text and image comprehension. In contrast, Flickr30k shows high discrepancies in fewer parameters, as it primarily involves text comprehension. For output-related patterns, we examine the absolute discrepancy in the deep (the last 50%) layers according to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Donahue et al., 2014</a>)</cite>. Text-output tasks (<span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, ImageNet, Grounding) concentrate their discrepancies in a small set of parameters primarily associated with text-generation, whereas image-output tasks (<span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, Flickr30k, HQEdit) exhibit discrepancies in another different and small set of parameters tied to image-generation. Notably, the overlap between text- and image-output related parameters remains isolated.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18055v1/pre.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:286/164;" width="286" height="164"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Results of different LoRA settings.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by the discovery, we propose two types of LoRA: General LoRA for modality comprehension and Expert LoRA for modality generation. General LoRA includes Image General LoRA for understanding images and Text General LoRA for understanding text. Similarly, Expert LoRA includes Image Expert LoRA for image generation and Text Expert LoRA for text generation. Considering that fine-tuning all LoRAs may lead to severe catastrophic forgetting, and the model primarily focuses on a particular subset of parameters in the specific task, we propose fine-tuning only the LoRA related to the task’s input and output modalities while freezing others. This approach enables learning the new task while preserving existing knowledge. For validation, we first fine-tune the LoRA on VQAv2 and then on Flickr30k. We adopt three settings: (<span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i</span>) LoRA, (<span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ii</span>) 2-Split LoRA splitting into two parts and updating according to the task-specific input modality, (<span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">iii</span>) 4-Split LoRA splitting into four parts and updating according to both the task-specific input and output modalities. The total rank of the three types of LoRA is the same. As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Motivation ‣ 4 MAGE: An Efficient UCL Framework ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, the proposed method (<span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">iii</span>) can achieve the best anti-forgetting ability with fewer reductions in new task learning performance.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18055v1/Figure3.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:499/166;" width="499" height="166" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of the MAGE. We insert four types of LoRA into the MLLM, Image/Text General LoRA (G-LoRA) and Image/Text Expert LoRA (E-LoRA). Then, we use the parameter-wise EMA strategy to update LoRA corresponding to the specific input and output modality of current task, while freezing that unrelated to it.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, we integrate General LoRA and Expert LoRA through an equal-weight linear summation as in Eq.(<a href="#S4.E1" title="In 4.1 Motivation ‣ 4 MAGE: An Efficient UCL Framework ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m1" h=(\mathcal{W}_{o}+\mathcal{W}_{down}^{GI}\mathcal{W}_{up}^{GI}+\mathcal{W}_{down}^{GT}\mathcal{W}_{up}^{GT}+\mathcal{W}_{down}^{EI}\mathcal{W}_{up}^{EI}+\mathcal{W}_{down}^{ET}\mathcal{W}_{up}^{ET})\,x.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Notably, although the frozen LoRA still participates in the prediction, it remains inactive and therefore does not influence the output. This design ensures that trainable LoRA facilitates cross-modal knowledge transfer while frozen LoRA prevents forgetting of modality-specific knowledge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Discussion<span id="S4.SS1.p6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">:</span></span> We analyze parameter update patterns across tasks with varying input–output modalities. Based on this insight, we propose MAGE, which explicitly separates modality comprehension components from modality generation components via structured LoRA specialization. This empirical observation serves as a motivating insight rather than a definitive conclusion. It highlights a practical direction for structuring parameter-efficient adaptations in continual learning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Mechanism of Anti-Forgetting</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To further mitigate forgetting, we draw inspiration from the Dynamic Exponential Moving Average (DEMA) method proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. However, its original setting is limited in 1) requiring a differencing-based approximation of the Hessian matrix, leading to introduce additional memory overhead (<span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, storing historical parameters and gradients), 2) relying on regularization to calculate EMA weights, resulting in a coarse, layer-wise granularity. To address these limitations, we revisit the derivation of dynamic EMA and propose a novel PEMA (Parameter-wise EMA) method.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kirkpatrick et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, we utilize the Fisher matrix to replace with Hessian matrix because the Fisher matrix equals the negative expected Hessian matrix. Leveraging Monte Carlo sampling to approximate this expectation, we compute the Fisher matrix by averaging the gradients of each sample in one mini-batch as shown in:</p>
<table id="S4.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\approx F_{ii}=\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{x\in B}\left(\left.\frac{\partial L(y,f(x))}{\partial\theta}\right|_{\theta=\theta_{t}}\right)^{2}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>≈</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></munder><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>|</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\approx F_{ii}=\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{x\in B}\left(\left.\frac{\partial L(y,f(x))}{\partial\theta}\right|_{\theta=\theta_{t}}\right)^{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> is the Fisher matrix, <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> denotes one mini-batch, <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> refers to the loss function, <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math> means the input and label, <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> represents the model and <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> indicates the parameters trained after task <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The calculation of dynamic EMA weight requires the inverse Hessian. Since the Hessian matrix is not always invertible, we adopt a regularized inverse way, as shown in Eq.(<a href="#S4.E3" title="In 4.2 Mechanism of Anti-Forgetting ‣ 4 MAGE: An Efficient UCL Framework ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). We add a term <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda I</annotation></semantics></math> to the Hessian matrix, where <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> is a hyperparameter (set to 1e-5) and <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the identity matrix. This procedure is equivalent to applying “damping” to the Hessian matrix, making nearly singular directions invertible and preventing numerically unstable exploding inverses, thereby ensuring that the modified Hessian matrix <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{H}</annotation></semantics></math> is always invertible.</p>
<table id="S4.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{H}=H^{T}H+\lambda I." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{H}=H^{T}H+\lambda I.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we obtain the parameter-wise EMA weights through matrix multiplication as in Eq.(<a href="#S4.E4" title="In 4.2 Mechanism of Anti-Forgetting ‣ 4 MAGE: An Efficient UCL Framework ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
<table id="S4.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{t}=[\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta_{t}}+I][(\theta_{t}-\theta_{t-1}^{*})^{T}\hat{H}]^{-1}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{t}=[\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta_{t}}+I][(\theta_{t}-\theta_{t-1}^{*})^{T}\hat{H}]^{-1},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{t-1}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{t-1}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is the EMA parameters trained after task <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t-1</annotation></semantics></math>. We utilize the PEMA method to update LoRA corresponding to the specific input and output modality of the current task. Detailed deduction process is in Appendix <a href="#Sx1.SS6" title="9.6 Mathematical Deduction ‣ Appendix ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9.6</span></a>. Comparisons between PEMA and DEMA are in Appendix <a href="#Sx1.SS8" title="9.8 Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9.8</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<td id="S5.T1.7.1.20.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:5pt;padding-bottom:5pt;"><span id="S5.T1.7.1.20.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;">47.88</span></td>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Implementation Details:</span> We adopt SEED-X <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ge et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> as our backbone with inserted LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> in the LLM side, LLaMA2-chat-13B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. During the unified comprehension and generation continual learning, we freeze the vision encoder and LLM, with only training connection layers and LoRA (Detailed information is listed in Appendix <a href="#Sx1.SS3" title="9.3 Training Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9.3</span></a>). The continual learning orders are VQAv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goyal et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, ImageNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite>, Flickr30k <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Plummer et al., 2015</a>)</cite>, OCRVQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mishra et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, RefCOCO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kazemzadeh et al., 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mao et al., 2016</a>)</cite>, and HQEdit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hui et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compared Methods<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">1</span></span>
                
                
                
              <span id="footnote1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">All methods hold an equal scale of trainable parameters.</span></span></span></span>:</span> (1) Zero-Shot, (2) LoRA Fine-Tune <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, (3) MoELoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, (4) LAE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, (5) EWC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kirkpatrick et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, (6) PGP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, (7) CIA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, (8) RegLoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Details are in Appendix <a href="#Sx1.SS4" title="9.4 Baseline Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Compared with baselines</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare the performance of our method with baselines in Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Under non-model-expansion settings, we observe that MAGE outperforms the best among other methods, CIA by +1.59@Avg.ACC and -2.63@Forgetting. Compared with LoRA Fine-Tune, MoELoRA has superior anti-forgetting performance due to the multi-experts mixture mechanism, while it fails in some tasks. Although methods like LAE and PGP can resist forgetting, their plasticity is influenced. EWC can perform well both in stability and plasticity, while the Avg.ACC needs to be improved. CIA and RegLoRA own both extraordinary new task learning and old task anti-forgetting abilities, while they require saving intermediate variables, leading to high memory consumption. MAGE outperforms all other baselines with less memory usage.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Forgetting Analysis</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We perform an in-depth analysis of forgetting in UCL and discover that it is mainly caused by three categories. The first category is instruction unfollowing, which refers to the model’s failure to follow input instructions when generating responses. We attribute this issue to semantic discrepancies among the instructions. The second category is hallucination, which means the model can not perform accurate predictions based on existing knowledge, resulting in the production of factually incorrect or illusory content. We consider hallucination to arise from the interference between new and old knowledge during continual task adaptation. Compared to instruction unfollowing, hallucination responses generally align well with the syntactic or structural demands of the instruction, while significantly differing from the ground truth. All other errors that do not fall into the above two categories are classified in the third category, presented as the other errors. Note that cases exhibiting both hallucination and instruction unfollowing are uniformly deemed instruction unfollowing errors.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18055v1/Figure5.png" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/384;" width="548" height="384" alt="Refer to caption">

</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We compare the performance of MAGE, MoELoRA, and LoRA Fine-Tune under Avg.HAL, Avg.IUF and Avg.OTH metrics in Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.3 Forgetting Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. With the multi-experts mixture mechanism, MoELoRA alleviates overall forgetting compared to LoRA Fine-Tune. Our method achieves notable reductions in Avg.HAL and Avg.IUF, while slight increases in Avg.OTH. This can be attributed to errors originally caused by hallucination and instruction unfollowing being transferred to the other error. These experiments provide explanations for the superior anti-forgetting ability of MAGE.</p>
</div>

<td id="S5.T4.7.1.6.10" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:5.2pt;padding-bottom:5.2pt;"><span id="S5.T4.7.1.6.10.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:207%;">59.79</span></td></tr>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Knowledge Transfer</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We investigate the knowledge transfer phenomenon in UCL, as shown in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.3 Forgetting Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. We primarily analyze intra-modal knowledge transfer, which occurs between tasks sharing similar instruction templates. To verify the effect of knowledge transfer in text modality, we evaluate performance on VQAv2 (Task 1) by using models trained on Flickr30k (Task 3) and OCRVQA (Task 4), respectively. In LoRA Fine-Tune, we observe that after training on Flickr30k, MLLM retains 20.10 accuracy on VQAv2, indicating a severe loss of previously learned knowledge. However, after training on OCRVQA, Accuracy on VQAv2 significantly improves to 50.26. This can be attributed to the knowledge transfer between OCRVQA and VQAv2, allowing the model to “recall” what it had previously learned in VQAv2. In MAGE, we witness a similar phenomenon after training on OCRVQA, the model’s performance on VQAv2 also has a substantial improvement. Notably, after training on Flickr30k, MAGE maintains a much higher Accuracy on VQAv2 (43.56) compared to LoRA Fine-Tune (20.10), which demonstrates the strong anti-forgetting capability of our method.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We further explore cross-modal knowledge transfer, which appears between tasks with similar semantics across modalities. We evaluate on Flickr30k by using models trained on Flickr30k and OCRVQA. Results confirm that training on OCRVQA further improves MLLMs’ performance on Flickr30k rather than degrading on this task, suggesting efficient text-to-image knowledge transfer. These findings resonate with some novel viewpoints in continual learning, like MLLMs do not really forget previous knowledge, and previous task capabilities could be restored through adaptation to new tasks. The observed knowledge transfer phenomena may provide experimental support and research perspectives for these opinions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5 </span>Robust Performance</h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To validate the robustness of MAGE, we adopt three training orders (Detailed information is in Appendix <a href="#Sx1.SS5" title="9.5 Training Orders ‣ Appendix ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9.5</span></a>). In Table <a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 5.5 Robust Performance ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we find that New.ACC and Avg.ACC have an observed range of fluctuations. Forgetting, as an important performance metric, has a small range of variation (from 12.17 to 12.35). Based on the observations, we conclude that the fluctuations in New.ACC and Avg.ACC are caused by changes in the task training order. However, our method has strong robustness, maintaining the Forgetting metric at a stable level.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 5</span>: </span><span id="S5.T5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">UCL performance under different task orders.</span></figcaption>

<section id="S5.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.6 </span>Ablation Studies</h3>

<div id="S5.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We progressively incorporate proposed modules to evaluate their contributions, starting from the simple MoELoRA baseline with four experts. Experimental results are shown in Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5.3 Forgetting Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. First, we replace the routing function in MoELoRA with an equal-weighted summation of outputs from LoRA experts and the base model (denoted as EW). This module increases the Avg.ACC from 43.90 to 46.75 and reduces the Forgetting from 19.08 to 15.66. Then, we introduce the General LoRA and Expert LoRA fusion mechanism (denoted as EW+GA) by increasing the Avg.ACC from 46.75 to 47.67 and decreasing the Forgetting from 15.66 to 14.90. Finally, we adopt the parameter-wise EMA update strategy (denoted as MAGE), which increases the Avg.ACC up to 49.58 and lowers the Forgetting to 12.26. Ablation studies demonstrate that each of the proposed modules contributes independently and significantly to the overall performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.7 </span>Descriptive Statistics</h3>

<div id="S5.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A full continual learning and evaluation pipeline spanning six tasks takes about one week to complete by using 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. We report the descriptive statistics about our results in Appendix <a href="#Sx1.SS8" title="9.8 Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix ‣ Continual-NExT: A Unified Comprehension And Generation Continual Learning Framework" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9.8</span></a> under distinct random seed settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the continual learning ability of Dual-to-Dual MLLMs, we establish a novel framework, Continual-NExT, with well-defined evaluation metrics. Furthermore, we discover that activated parameters are closely related to input modalities and output modalities of the training task and propose an efficient MAGE method. Additionally, we propose a fine-grained and parameter-wise EMA method to mitigate forgetting. Experiments show that our method has excellent anti-forgetting ability and continual learning performance. In the future, we aim to extend our framework and method to more modalities and stronger Any-to-Any MLLMs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Limitations</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For limitations, as the number of modalities is incrementally growing, the corresponding increase in the number of LoRA experts may lead to a linear explosion in both computational cost and memory consumption. Note that both image and text are seen modalities for the adopted MLLM backbone, whether MLLMs can incrementally incorporate unseen modalities remains an open question. Our future research will focus on how to effectively address the above challenges. Additionally, we note that alternative decompositions, such as finer-grained splits, hierarchical structures, or dynamically routed adaptations, are plausible extensions, and we leave their exploration to future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Ethical Considerations</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This work proposes a continual learning framework for unified comprehension and generation using publicly available datasets. The proposed method does not introduce new data sources or application scenarios beyond standard benchmarks, and thus does not raise additional ethical concerns beyond those inherent to the underlying pretrained models and datasets. Potential risks include the propagation of biases present in the pretrained models, as well as possible performance degradation in safety-critical or out-of-distribution settings. We do not evaluate our method in high-risk real-world applications, and recommend caution when deploying the framework in such scenarios.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">All datasets used in this work are publicly available benchmarks that have been widely used in prior research. We do not collect any new data, and the datasets do not contain personally identifying information beyond what is already present in the original releases. We follow the original dataset licenses and usage guidelines, and do not perform any additional data processing that would introduce privacy risks. As such, our work does not raise new concerns regarding personal data or offensive content beyond those associated with existing benchmarks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S9" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">9 </span>Conclusion</h2>

</section>

<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Appendix</h2>

<section id="Sx1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">9.1 </span>Task and Dataset Details</h3>

<div id="Sx1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">VQAv2</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>: The Visual Question Answering v2.0 (VQA v2.0) dataset is a widely used multimodal benchmark. It is designed to evaluate a model’s ability to answer open-ended questions about images, requiring an understanding of both visual content and language based upon the MS COCO dataset. Each question is associated with 10 ground truth answers provided by human annotators, capturing the variability in human responses. Each image has an average of 5.4 questions, covering a wide range of topics and difficulty levels. The dataset has been instrumental in advancing research in visual question answering, promoting the development of models that integrate visual perception with language understanding.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ImageNet</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>: The ImageNet-1K dataset, also known as the ILSVRC 2012 dataset, is a foundational benchmark in computer vision. It comprises 1,000 distinct object categories. These categories include a diverse array of objects such as animals, vehicles, and everyday items, providing a comprehensive resource for training and evaluating image classification models.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Flickr30k</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>: The Flickr30k dataset is a widely used benchmark for tasks involving image generation. It consists of images sourced from Flickr, each annotated with five human-generated descriptions. These annotations cover a diverse range of scenes and activities, making the dataset valuable for training and evaluating models that generate images of natural language descriptions.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OCRVQA</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>: The OCR-VQA dataset is a large-scale benchmark designed to advance the field of Visual Question Answering (VQA) by focusing on questions that require reading and understanding text within images. Unlike traditional VQA datasets that emphasize object recognition and scene understanding, OCR-VQA challenges models to extract and interpret textual information from images. Questions in the dataset pertain to details such as the book’s title, author, genre, and publication year, necessitating the integration of Optical Character Recognition (OCR) techniques with natural language understanding. The dataset serves as a valuable resource for developing models capable of reading and reasoning over textual content in images.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RefCOCO</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>: The RefCOCO dataset is a widely used benchmark in vision-and-language research, focusing on referring expression comprehension (REC)—the task of identifying a specific object in an image based on a natural language description. Built upon images from the MS COCO dataset, RefCOCO provides annotations that link textual expressions to corresponding objects within images. RefCOCO comprises three primary subsets: RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg. The RefCOCO series has been instrumental in advancing research in referring expression comprehension and related tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">HQEdit</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>: The HQEdit dataset is a high-quality, instruction-based image editing dataset designed to advance the field of vision-language models. It comprises meticulously curated image editing instances, each consisting of an input image, a detailed textual editing instruction, and the corresponding output image. Developed using a scalable pipeline that leverages advanced foundation models such as GPT-4V and DALLE 3, HQEdit ensures high-resolution images rich in detail. The dataset includes comprehensive editing prompts and inverse-edit instructions, facilitating nuanced understanding and manipulation of visual content.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The adopted dataset statistics are as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">•<span id="Sx1.SS1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">VQAv2 Task:</span> 82,783 samples for training, 5,000 samples for testing.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">•<span id="Sx1.SS1.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ImageNet Task:</span> 129,833 samples for training, 5,050 samples for testing.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">•<span id="Sx1.SS1.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Flickr30k Task:</span> 30,783 samples for training, 1,000 samples for testing.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS1.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS1.p11.1" class="ltx_p">•<span id="Sx1.SS1.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OCRVQA Task:</span> 164,948 samples for training, 5,000 samples for testing.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS1.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS1.p12.1" class="ltx_p">•<span id="Sx1.SS1.p12.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RefCOCO Task:</span> 53,700 samples for training, 5,000 samples for testing.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS1.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS1.p13.1" class="ltx_p">•<span id="Sx1.SS1.p13.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">HQEdit Task:</span> 8,813 samples for training, 1,000 samples for testing.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx1.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18055v1/Figure7.png" id="Sx1.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/180;" width="548" height="180" alt="Refer to caption">

</div>

<div id="Sx1.SS1.p16" class="ltx_para">

<div id="Sx1.SS1.p18" class="ltx_para">

<div id="Sx1.SS1.p19" class="ltx_para">

<div id="Sx1.SS1.p21" class="ltx_para">

When the provided information is insufficient, respond with ’Unanswerable’. Answer each question using a single word or phrase.", "answer": "Amy Knapp"</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS1.p26" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS1.p26.1" class="ltx_p">•<span id="Sx1.SS1.p26.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RefCOCO Task:</span> "question id": "34136", "size": [640,424], "image": "xxx.jpg", "text": "Please provide the bounding box coordinate of the region this sentence describes: tennis player.", "origin answer bbox": "[242.94,155.68,86.22,162.53]", "answer bbox": "[0.38,0.41,0.51,0.67]"</p>

</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS1.p28" class="ltx_para">

</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">9.2 </span>Metric Details</h3>

<div id="Sx1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Average Accuracy</span> (Avg.ACC) measures the mean test accuracy over all tasks, providing an overall assessment of the model’s performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Forgetting</span> (FOR) quantifies the degradation in performance on previously learned tasks after the model acquires new knowledge, thus characterizing stability.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">New Accuracy</span> (New.ACC) computes the average test accuracy on newly introduced tasks, serving as an indicator of the model’s plasticity.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, Average Accuracy, Forgetting, and New Accuracy are generally defined as:</p>
<table id="Sx1.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="Sx1.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Avg.ACC}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^{T}A_{T,i}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Avg.ACC</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>T</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Avg.ACC}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^{T}A_{T,i},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<table id="Sx1.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="Sx1.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{FOR}=\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{i=1}^{T-1}{A_{T,i}-\text{max}(A_{j,i})_{j\in[i,T-1]}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>FOR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mtext>max</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{FOR}=\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{i=1}^{T-1}{A_{T,i}-\text{max}(A_{j,i})_{j\in[i,T-1]}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<table id="Sx1.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="Sx1.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{New.ACC}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^{T}A_{i,i}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>New.ACC</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>T</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{New.ACC}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^{T}A_{i,i},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Sx1.SS2.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="Sx1.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of tasks, <math id="Sx1.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{T,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{T,i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the accuracy of <math id="Sx1.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th task on the model trained after <math id="Sx1.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>-th task, <math id="Sx1.SS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{j,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{j,i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the accuracy of <math id="Sx1.SS2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th task on the model trained after <math id="Sx1.SS2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>-th task, and <math id="Sx1.SS2.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{i,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{i,i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the accuracy of <math id="Sx1.SS2.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th task on the model trained after <math id="Sx1.SS2.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th task.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Average Hallucination</span> (Avg.HAL) is utilized to depict hallucination-related forgetting.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Average Instruction Unfollowing</span> (Avg.IUF) is designed for showing instruction unfollowing-related forgetting.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.SS2.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Average Other Error</span> (Avg.OTH) is proposed to summarize the other errors of forgetting.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, Average Hallucination, Average Instruction Unfollowing, and Average Other Error are defined as:</p>
<table id="Sx1.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
